title: Keep learning
whyMatters: The first word revealed in the Quran was 'Iqra', which means Read. Islam puts unusual weight on seeking knowledge. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) said, 'Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.' Your learning will never actually finish, and that is one of the better things about this faith. Now that prayer, community, and daily practice are settling into place, this is the point to go deeper and build a base of knowledge you will use for the rest of your life.

subSteps: Many masjids in Toronto run weekly halaqas, small group sessions where a teacher works through Quran, hadith, or a single topic.
They are friendly rooms and questions are welcome.
Ask your local masjid about classes for new Muslims, because many run a dedicated program.
If in-person options are thin where you are, look for online halaqas through organizations like AlMaghrib Institute, Yaqeen Institute, or SeekersGuidance.
Turning up regularly beats going hard once. One class a week does more than a lecture binge every month.

exactActions.text: Work out which sources to trust
subSteps: Plenty of Islamic content online is either inaccurate or pitched at the wrong level for you. Stick to sources that have been vetted.
Worth starting with: Yaqeen Institute for research-based articles and videos, SeekersGuidance for free structured courses, and Bayyinah for Quran and Arabic.
Look for scholars and teachers who are qualified, balanced, and compassionate.
Be wary of social media accounts that live on controversy or extreme positions, because they rarely represent mainstream Islam.
When you are unsure about a source, ask your imam or your mentor what they think of it.
Start with accessible introductions rather than dense scholarly works.
'Being Muslim: A Practical Guide' by Asad Tarsin: a modern, practical overview.
'The Sealed Nectar' (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum) by Safiur Rahman Mubarakpuri: a widely read biography of the Prophet.
'Purification of the Heart' by Hamza Yusuf: on inner spiritual development.
'In the Footsteps of the Prophet' by Tariq Ramadan: a reflective seerah.
Read at your own pace. A few pages a week adds up faster than you expect.
A real connection with a teacher speeds up your learning and heads off misunderstandings.
Go to lectures or Friday khutbahs at different masjids to hear more than one perspective.
If you can, sign up for a structured course, even a free online one, instead of collecting bits from random articles.
A good teacher gives you the context and answers the question you actually asked.
Remember the hadith: 'Whoever travels a path seeking knowledge, Allah will make easy for them a path to Paradise.'
Decide what you want next, whether that is the basics of Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh), closer Quran study, or the stories of the prophets.
Set something achievable: one book this month, one new surah memorized, one online course finished.
Keep a record, because seeing the distance you have covered keeps you going.
Pass on what you learn, even as a beginner. Teaching something makes you understand it better.
Mark the milestones. Every piece of knowledge you pick up is a gift.

timeEstimate: Ongoing. Give at least 30 minutes a week to structured learning

obstacles.problem: I find conflicting information and don't know what to trust
obstacles.solution: This frustrates almost every new Muslim. Islam has several schools of thought (madhabs), and scholars differ on secondary questions. Get the agreed-upon material down first: the pillars of faith, the pillars of Islam, core ethics. Where there is disagreement, follow one teacher or one school rather than blending opinions together. In time you will be able to weigh different positions yourself. When you are stuck, ask your imam.

obstacles.problem: I feel overwhelmed by how much there is to learn
obstacles.solution: Islam is a tradition more than 1,400 years deep, and nobody learns all of it. Treat it as a lifelong path rather than a race. You already have the parts that matter most: your Shahada, your prayers, and your intention to please Allah. Everything else gets built on top of that. Learn what your life needs right now and widen out from there.

obstacles.problem: I don't have access to a teacher or scholar
obstacles.solution: In-person learning is better, but what is available online now is genuinely useful. SeekersGuidance runs free structured courses with qualified teachers. Yaqeen Institute publishes research-backed material. Channels like Nouman Ali Khan's Bayyinah TV explain the Quran well. Many scholars take questions online. Start there, and keep looking for a local mentor as you settle into your community.

obstacles.problem: I feel too shy to ask questions
obstacles.solution: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said, 'The cure for ignorance is to ask.' Your questions are not silly, they are what a sincere heart sounds like. If asking in a group is too much, catch the teacher privately afterwards. Write your questions down beforehand. Some online platforms let you ask anonymously. Every knowledgeable Muslim you admire was once standing exactly where you are.

obstacles.problem: I get bored or lose motivation to study
obstacles.solution: Change the format. If reading feels heavy, watch something instead. If lectures drag, put a podcast on during your commute. If studying alone is lonely, join a group. Pick subjects you are actually curious about, whether that is the stories of the prophets, Islamic history, or how hadith are verified. Once something has your attention, the motivation follows. And on the flat days, a five-minute reminder still counts.

tinyVersion: Pick one reliable source, a book or a course or a weekly class, and stay with it. Small amounts done regularly add up to real understanding.
unlocksNext: With knowledge and practice under you, you are ready for the pillars still ahead, Zakat and Hajj, and for thinking about your longer-term goals as a Muslim.
